highlights.text: four basic senses: (1) slowness and its kin (forbearance, deliberation); (2) an hour of time; (3) a thing's reaching or ripening; (4) a vessel
highlights.note: Ibn Faris's four origins of the root

highlights.text: Al-inā / al-anā is an hour, especially of the night; plural ānāʾ
Al-ināʾ (with long final alif) is a container, from al-āniyah (vessels)
lam yaʾni laka = "the time has not come for you"
al-Nābigha: "deliberation is felicity — proceed deliberately and you will succeed"
the Prophet's words to a man who climbed over people on Friday — «you caused harm (ādhayta) and delayed (ānayta)» — glossed as "you came late and were slow"
highlights.note: a hadith, glossed for the sense "to be slow"

highlights.text: four core senses, from which all its derived words branch out
highlights.note: Ibn Faris's statement of the root's origins

highlights.text: Al-arab means "need" (al-Khalīl): "mā arabuka ilā hādhā" — "what do you need this for?"
highlights.note: إِرْبَة / مَـَارِب, the sense of need

highlights.text: The nouns maʾraba, maʾruba, and irba likewise all mean "need."
The entry cites Qur'an 24:31, {ghayri ulī l-irbati min al-rijāl} ("...those among men who have no irba..."), as an instance of this sense
the proverb "arabun lā ḥafāwatun" ("need, not warm regard"): said of someone whose visit is prompted by need rather than affection
highlights.note: proverb, for the sense the Qur'an uses

highlights.text: illustrated with a verse of Qays on growing skilled at repelling war
cited in a ḥadīth: "muʾārabatu l-arībi jahlun" — "to try to outwit the shrewd man is folly."
A ḥadīth uses irb for "limb": "kāna amlakakum li-irbihi" — "most in command of his own body/limbs."
Ibn Fāris treats أ-ر-ك as two independent roots, from which everything else branches
the couch or bed set inside the curtained canopy (ḥajala) is called أَرِيكَة (arīka), plural أَرَائِك (arāʾik)
Shāhid from Abū Dhuʾayb on choosing "the milk of the ārikāt in summer."
A ḥadīth is cited in which the Prophet was brought, at ʿArafa, the milk of awārik camels.
highlights.note: a hadith, cited for awarik camels

highlights.text: a single root whose core notion is something being missed or lost
to grieve or feel bitter regret over something
الأَسِف means "the angry one."
al-Aʿshā describing "a man of them asīf, as though pressing to his flanks a hand dyed [red]"
Two distinct roots:
highlights.note: the entry gives two separate origins

highlights.text: asina al-māʾ — water changes/spoils (becomes stale)
"min māʾin ghayri āsin" — "from water unaltered [in taste or smell]"
confining, holding fast, restraining
anyone taken/seized was called أَسِير even if he was not actually tied up
poetry "has fettered me in its bayt (house/verse) as the binding cords fetter the wild ass."
the foundation or base of a built thing
"he built his house on its original foundation" (أساس)
"Whoever does not found (yuʾassis) his dominion on justice has already demolished it"
highlights.note: the verb the Qur'an uses, yuʾassis

highlights.text: a single root meaning to treat/heal and to set right
لِي فِي فُلَانٍ أُسْوَةٌ = "so-and-so is a قُدْوَة (qudwa) for me," i.e. "I model myself on him."
"They are the ones who treat the umm al-raʾs [deep head wound] when the physicians and the healers passed it off on one another"
"to come." أَتَانِي فُلَانٌ = "so-and-so came to me."
highlights.note: Ibn Faris's core sense of the root

highlights.text: الإِيتَاء = "giving" (آتَى يُؤْتِي إِيتَاءً)
A line of al-Nābigha is cited, with two interpretations of أَتِيّ (the watercourse of a tent-trench, or the debris damming it)
Cited verses (including Labīd) use تَأْتَى as a lightened form of تَأَتَّى.
the ḥadīth of Thābit b. al-Daḥdāḥ, «إنما هو أتيٌّ فينا» ("he is only a newcomer among us")
the root/origin of a thing, and its accumulation.
al-athl — a literal tree, described by al-Khalīl (resembling tamarisk, but larger, with better wood used for fine cups)
illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Aʿshā daring an opponent to keep trying and failing to harm him
slowness and lagging behind
the person who bears sin is one who is "slow toward the good and lags behind it."
أَثِيمٌ (athīm) and أَثُومٌ (athūm) describe a man deeply given to sin.
"when the lagging she-camels belie the midday heat"
Some transmit from al-Akhfash that al-ithm means wine (khamr), reading Qurʾān 7:33 ("...and al-ithm") accordingly
highlights.note: al-Akhfash's reading of Q 7:33; Ibn Faris doubts it

highlights.text: (1) giving something precedence, (2) mentioning or reporting something, and (3) the lasting mark or trace a thing leaves behind
الأَثَر: the visible remnant of anything, or the lingering residue of what is not seen
آثَرْتُهُ إِيثَارًا, "I preferred him,"
الأَثَارَة = a remnant of a thing (plural أَثَارَات), as in {أَوْ أَثَارَةٍ مِنْ عِلْمٍ} "or a remnant/trace of knowledge" (46:4)
Cited in a line of ʿUrwa b. al-Ward.
Proverb: «تدع العين وتطلب الأثر» — leaving the spring for the track, i.e. forsaking ease for hardship.
Ḥadīth: «سَتَرَوْنَ بَعْدِي أَثَرَةً» — "you will see people take the spoils (fayʾ) for themselves."
highlights.note: a hadith, for athara as self-preference

highlights.text: ʿUmar's ḥadīth «ما حلفت بعدها آثِرًا ولا ذاكِرًا»: آثِر = reporting another's oath
highlights.note: a hadith of ʿUmar, for athir as "reporting"

highlights.text: abundance, bulk. Al-athāth, al-athāthah, al-uthūth all denote abundance/largeness "of anything."
Al-athāth = wealth, goods, household furnishings.
the Qur'anic phrase "athāthan wa ri'yā" (19:74) is glossed by al-Farrāʾ and Abū Zayd simply as matāʿ, "goods/furnishings"
Imruʾ al-Qays uses it of hair, comparing it to a date-palm cluster heavy with fruit.
a single core idea: returning (rujūʿ)
Al-maʾāb = the place of return.
Al-taʾwīb also = glorifying/praising (tasbīḥ), which Ibn Fāris links to the Qurʾanic "O mountains, echo/return [praise] with him, and the birds" (Saba 34:10)
iyāb just means returning at any time (قد آب المسافر = the traveller has returned)
citing ʿAbīd's line "every absent one returns…"
bending and curving.
ādanī al-shayʾu yaʾūdunī — an idiom for something weighing heavily on you
the letters hamza-waw-ha do not form a true triliteral root
highlights.note: the entry denies the root a common sense

highlights.text: ta'awwaha means "he uttered a sigh," specifically by saying "awwah" or "awhi"
Ibn Faris glosses awwah as ad-Da'daa' - one who supplicates/invokes (God) frequently
two base ideas: (1) the beginning of a matter, and (2) its end / return
highlights.note: Ibn Faris's two origins of the root

highlights.text: أَوَّل (awwal) is the outset of a thing.
آل الرجل = a man's household/kin, because their destination is to him and his to them
تَأْوِيل of speech = its outcome, what it "comes back to."
the sense of the vocative يَالَ فُلَان ("O people of…", shāhid, Ṭarafa)
Ibn Fāris reads Q 7:53 {هل ينظرون إلا تأويله} as "what it comes to at the resurrection,"
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 7:53

highlights.text: (1) gathering / coming together, and (2) tenderness / compassion
أَوَى (awā): a person betakes himself to his dwelling
المأوى (al-maʾwā): the place to which anything betakes itself or takes shelter
the core of akhadha is taking possession of a thing: gathering it in and collecting it
al-Khalīl defines akhdh as the opposite of giving, that is, taking hold of something.
a line by ʿAdī ibn Zayd describing rain, recited by Abū ʿUbayd and others, in which the pools are "not sparing with the ikhādh"
Masrūq ibn al-Ajdaʿ's comparison of the companions of Muḥammad to such pools
highlights.note: a saying of Masruq b. al-Ajdaʿ

highlights.text: the opposite of precedence or coming-forward
al-ākhir ("the last, the latter") is the contrary of "the one going before,"
ukhar is the plural of the feminine ukhrā ("others")
the cited line "I am the one born in the rear of the camels" (ukhrā al-ibil)
"brother." أَخ (akh, brother); dual أَخَوان (akhawān, two brothers); plurals إِخوة (ikhwa) and إِخوان (ikhwān)
The feminine of akh is أُخْت (ukht, sister)
two linked ideas: strength and protection
The verb أَيَّدَهُ (ayyadahu) means "he strengthened him"
three unrelated meanings: smoke, the snake, and the spouseless person
highlights.note: Ibn Faris gives the root three origins

highlights.text: Al-ayyim is a woman without a husband, or a man without a wife.
Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an, "And marry off the ayāmā among you" (Q24:32), as the attestation.
The poet Abū Dhuʾayb pictures a beekeeper smoking out a hive
the root ʾ-y-y (hamza–yāʾ–yāʾ) from two distinct origins
highlights.note: Ibn Faris's two origins of the root

highlights.text: From this second origin comes آية = a sign or mark (علامة).
Ibn Fāris explains آية القرآن (a Qurʾānic āya) as "a group of letters"
تَأَيَّيْتُ [الأمرَ] = "you waited for the moment it became possible" (with a verse of ʿAdī)
a single core idea: **nearness, drawing close**
أَزِفَ الرَّحِيلُ — "the departure has drawn near," i.e. it has come close.
He cites Qur'an 53:57, {أَزِفَتِ الْآزِفَةُ} ("the Impending has drawn near")
describing a youth "cut to the cut of a sword — not *mutaʾāzif*, nor flabby in chest and shoulder-flesh,"
highlights.note: the mother of Yazid b. al-Tathriyya, Umayyad; no earlier witness

highlights.text: glosses الآزفة as the Resurrection
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 53:57
